newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar surges after CPI, seen thrusting higher.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar surges after CPI, seen thrusting higher.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar surged on Friday on worse than expected inflation data, with the Trade-Weighted Index closing at its highest levels since late 1987 and a chartist picking another sharp move higher.
The currency finished at US$0.7091/98 and 68.60 on the TWI, up from 0.7058/65 and 68.22 at the opening.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.7 percent for the December quarter and 2.6 percent for the year, while underlying inflation came in at 0.63 percent and 2.4 percent respectively.
The Reserve Bank had forecast core inflation at 0.5 percent for the quarter and 2.3 percent for the year, while economists expected 0.4 and 2.15 percent respectively.
The Kiwi traded as high as US$0.7105 on the news, which scotched prospects of a further monetary easing.

"The currency still seems pretty well bid. It seems that it's very hard to short it," an Auckland dealer said. There were stop-loss buy orders at 0.7115 and higher, and a break above 0.7110 could bump the currency up to the 0.7125-30 area.
Another saw support at 0.7065-70 and a likely near-term range of 0.7070-7120.
ANZ Bank technical analyst Mark Elliott said the currency was now well positioned for a strong move upwards.
"The technical position of the Kiwi is very strong and I would bet very strongly that we see a sharp move higher, probably into the 0.7200-50 window in the coming couple of weeks," he said.

Dealers said they were wary of possible comment next week from Treasurer Winston Peters, who promised during last year's election campaign to drive the dollar down, or from Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash.
They said that while the TWI was a lot higher than the Reserve Bank would like, spelling further pain for manufacturers and exporters, it was powerless to alter the mix of monetary conditions.

"It's the complete opposite to what they want. They've got a very strong currency and they've got bill rates probably lower than they would like, given that inflation data today, but there's really not much they can do about it, unfortunately," said Chris Rand, chief forex manager at Westpac.
"I think further down the track, the prospect of a weaker economy may well be the thing that triggers a lower currency and lower rates, but that's not going to happen in the near-term."
